advances: Gives an exact one-constraint finite dual obstruction to the proposed universal measure. This disproves only the auxiliary global-profile-minorant-measure assertion; it is not a counterexample to the locked centerpoint theorem.
author: mp_r215_profile_minorant
proof:
The triangle \(\Delta\) has area \(1\), and \(\tfrac12\Delta\) has area \(1/4\). Hence
\[
(a_0,a_1,a_2)=(1,1,\tfrac14),\qquad T=\tfrac94.
\]
The strict area-triangle inequalities are
\[
1<1+\tfrac14,\qquad 1<1+\tfrac14,\qquad \tfrac14<1+1.
\]

We verify compatibility without assuming any unlisted result. Since the first coordinate of \(C\) lies in \([0,2]\), its only integer values are \(0,1,2\). The sections at heights \(0\) and \(2\) are exactly \(A_0\) and \(A_2\), because a convex combination having an extreme height can use points only from the corresponding extreme section.

Also,
\[
\frac{A_0+A_2}{2}
=\frac{\Delta+\frac12\Delta}{2}
=\frac34\Delta
\subseteq\Delta=A_1,
\]
where the Minkowski identity follows from convexity of \(\Delta\), and the last inclusion follows from \(0\in\Delta\). To identify the height-\(1\) section, group any convex representation of a point of \(C\) by heights, with weights \(\theta_0,\theta_1,\theta_2\). The equations
\[
\theta_0+\theta_1+\theta_2=1,\qquad
\theta_1+2\theta_2=1
\]
give \(\theta_0=\theta_2=s\) and \(\theta_1=1-2s\). Its planar component therefore equals
\[
(1-2s)w_1+2s\,\frac{w_0+w_2}{2}
\]
for \(w_i\in A_i\), and belongs to \(A_1\) by the displayed midpoint inclusion and convexity. The reverse inclusion is part of the definition of \(C\). Thus the height-\(1\) section is exactly \(A_1\), so \(C\) is compatible with the locked problem.

Now take \(q=(1,0)\) and \(r=2\), writing the first planar coordinate as \(x\). Since \(A_1\subseteq\{x\le2\}\),
\[
F_{1,q}(2)=1.
\]
For every \(\lambda\ge0\), the threshold \(2+\lambda\) contains all of \(A_0\), so
\[
F_{0,q}(2+\lambda)+F_{2,q}(2-\lambda)\ge1.
\]
For every \(\lambda<0\), one has \(2-\lambda>2\), while the largest first coordinate in \(A_2=\tfrac12\Delta\) is \(1\). Hence the second cap contains all of \(A_2\), and
\[
F_{0,q}(2+\lambda)+F_{2,q}(2-\lambda)\ge\tfrac14.
\]
Taking \(\lambda=-3\) gives thresholds \(-1\) and \(5\), so the first cap is empty and the second is all of \(A_2\). Therefore
\[
\inf_{\lambda\in\mathbb R}
\bigl(F_{0,q}(2+\lambda)+F_{2,q}(2-\lambda)\bigr)=\tfrac14
\]
and consequently
\[
\Phi_q(2)=1+\tfrac14=\tfrac54.
\]
All caps here are closed; the chosen thresholds either contain the whole polygon or miss it, so there is no boundary issue.

For any finite Borel measure supported on \(A_1\), the halfplane
\(\{x\le2\}\) contains its entire support. Thus its single required profile inequality would give
\[
\nu(A_1)=\nu(\{x\le2\})\le\Phi_q(2)=\tfrac54.
\]
On the other hand, the required total mass is
\[
\nu(A_1)\ge\frac{2T}{3}
=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac94=\frac32.
\]
Since \(5/4<3/2\), no such measure exists. Equivalently, the finite dual certificate assigns multiplier \(1\) to the single halfplane constraint \((q,r)=((1,0),2)\); on measures supported on \(A_1\), its left side is exactly the total-mass objective and its right side is \(5/4\).

This contradiction concerns only the proposed auxiliary measure. It produces no point of mixed-integer depth below \(2T/9\) and hence is not a counterexample to the locked theorem.
statement:
Let
\[
\Delta=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(2,0),(0,1)\},\qquad
A_0=A_1=\Delta,\qquad A_2=\tfrac12\Delta,
\]
and let
\[
C=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((\{0\}\times A_0)\cup
(\{1\}\times A_1)\cup(\{2\}\times A_2)\bigr).
\]
Then \(C\) is a compact polytope compatible with the locked problem, its areas satisfy the strict area-triangle inequalities, but there is no finite Borel measure \(\nu\) supported on \(A_1\) such that
\[
\nu(A_1)\ge \frac{2(a_0+a_1+a_2)}3
\]
and, simultaneously for every \(q\in\mathbb S^1\) and \(r\in\mathbb R\),
\[
\nu(\{w:q\cdot w\le r\})\le
F_{1,q}(r)+\inf_{\lambda\in\mathbb R}
\bigl(F_{0,q}(r+\lambda)+F_{2,q}(r-\lambda)\bigr).
\]
The obstruction consists of the single constraint \(q=(1,0)\), \(r=2\).
